prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: Cross-tab · Regional sales (language en).
Grid: 7 columns × 5 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Region" · longest unbreakable word 57px · one-line width 195px
  col 2: header "Jan" · longest unbreakable word 38px · one-line width 38px
  col 3: header "Feb" · longest unbreakable word 38px · one-line width 38px
  col 4: header "Mar" · longest unbreakable word 38px · one-line width 38px
  col 5: header "Apr" · longest unbreakable word 38px · one-line width 38px
  col 6: header "May" · longest unbreakable word 38px · one-line width 38px
  col 7: header "Jun" · longest unbreakable word 38px · one-line width 38px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 490px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 489px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Region names remain intact, with only the long regional label wrapping; the six month columns are evenly paced and their values are easy to compare."},"B":{"grade":"excellent","why":"The row labels read cleanly, the long label wraps naturally, and the month columns have a consistent rhythm."},"C":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"The numbers align clearly, but the narrow region column wraps three labels and makes the rows taller without improving comparison."},"D":{"grade":"bad","why":"The region header and several names break within words, making row identification difficult and leaving excessive vertical space beside the figures."},"E":{"grade":"good","why":"Labels and values remain intact, but the month columns vary in width, giving equivalent measures a less consistent rhythm."}},"best":["A","B"],"confidence":"medium","unsure":"A and B appear nearly identical at the displayed size, so I cannot confidently distinguish their column proportions."}
